children.title: CFPB work stoppages and staff reductions begin
children.description_medium: In February 2025, acting CFPB leadership ordered broad work stoppages and the administration began terminating categories of employees. Reuters reported layoffs extending beyond probationary staff, and the employees’ union brought litigation challenging the changes. Those steps preceded the later partial resumption of legally required work.
children.description_long: Acting leadership at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered broad work stoppages, and the administration began terminating categories of CFPB employees in February 2025. Reuters reported on February 13 that layoffs were being broadened beyond probationary staff. The actions prompted litigation from the employees’ union. This was the start of a sequence of separate agency changes and court proceedings, not a legal dissolution of the CFPB. The supplied report supports describing the February work halt and staff reductions as actions underway and the union litigation as a response. It does not establish that all bureau work ceased or that every pending enforcement matter was dropped. In March, emails reported by Reuters showed that some work considered legally required resumed while the court challenge continued; that later development is recorded separately. The February event is thus limited to the initial stoppages and staff reductions reported at the time. Its publication date should not be mistaken for an exact order date, which the packet does not supply.
children.date_uncertainty: The proposal dates the initial actions to February 10; the supplied Reuters report was published February 13 and does not specify an exact order date.

children.title: Some CFPB work resumes amid court challenge
children.description_medium: On March 5, 2025, Reuters reported emails showing that the administration allowed several CFPB offices to resume functions officials considered legally required, while litigation over the bureau’s operations continued. The evidence undercuts the claim that the agency had simply ceased to exist; this was not a full return to normal operations.
children.description_long: Reuters reported on March 5, 2025, that emails showed the administration allowed several Consumer Financial Protection Bureau offices to resume functions officials considered legally required. This partial resumption took place amid a court battle over the administration’s actions at the bureau. The supplied source describes selected offices and functions returning to work; it does not say that all CFPB operations resumed or that the legal dispute had ended. It is a distinct point in the chronology between the February work stoppages and layoffs and the April attempt to dismiss most of the workforce. The emails are material because they show the agency continued to perform at least some functions during the litigation, contrary to a claim that it had simply ceased to exist. They do not establish the full scope of ongoing enforcement work or the status of every pending matter. This account therefore retains the limited finding: certain offices were allowed to resume functions officials regarded as legally required while the broader court challenge continued.
children.date_uncertainty: March 5 is the Reuters publication date for the reporting on emails; the emails’ dates are not specified in the packet.

children.title: Judge halts CFPB attempt to lay off most of its workforce
children.description_medium: In April 2025, the CFPB attempted to dismiss roughly 1,400 to 1,500 employees, potentially about 90% of its workforce. A federal judge halted the mass firings while litigation over compliance with earlier court orders continued; the agency was not legally disbanded. The layoffs were attempted, not completed.
children.description_long: The CFPB attempted to dismiss roughly 1,400 to 1,500 employees in April 2025, a reduction that could have removed about 90 percent of the bureau’s workforce. A federal judge temporarily halted the mass firings while litigation over the administration’s compliance with earlier court orders continued. Reuters reported the court action through Inc.com on April 20; the proposed event date in the packet is April 17. The supplied report supports describing an attempted mass layoff and a judicial halt, not a completed reduction of the workforce. This was a later development than the February stoppages and staff terminations and the partial resumption of certain legally required functions reported in March. Those separate stages should not be compressed into a claim that the agency was simply disbanded in August. The packet also says the evidence does not establish that all pending enforcement actions were dropped. The account therefore records the attempted April dismissals and the court’s temporary intervention, with timing qualified by the article publication date.
children.date_uncertainty: The proposal dates the attempted mass layoffs to April 17; the Reuters report was published April 20 and says a judge temporarily halted them.

unresolved_components.title: Claim that CFPB was legally disbanded and all pending enforcement actions were dropped
unresolved_components.reason: The packet says the CFPB remained in existence, litigation constrained mass layoffs, legally required work resumed in part, and the all-actions claim exceeds evidence.
unresolved_components.missing_evidence: A court order or other direct evidence showing legal dissolution and complete termination of every pending enforcement action.

rationale: The packet supports separate February, March, and April developments, with court action and work resumption reflected as separate stages. Publication dates are distinguished from dates of underlying actions where available.
